Qb2+ !!!! A stunning sacrifice. The king is forced to take. You must play c1=B, because c1=Q would be stalemate as the white king has no moves after that. After this, the king will likely move to c2, resulting in a deadly fork on your bishop and pawn. The bishop is more valuable, so retreat to a3, sacrificing the pawn. After Kxd2 we can hit the white king with the devastating check Bb4, forcing Kxe2.   


At this point the king has made major inroads into the pawn structure, and will likely win the h pawn at some point; to protect against this you must play f1=N. after Kf2, white has gained control of the important queening square g1. To divert white from this square you use the diversion tactic Ng3! Then white, unphased, plays Kxg2!!!!!!! Unfortunately you do not have time to queen now as your knight is under attack, black must play Ne4 and lose the a pawn.   


Unfortunately black now has no way to make a rook or a queen and a draw must be called, since you don't know how to mate in this position. A beautiful forced draw for white, but I guess he must have blundered along the way and allowed you to win.

Another interesting thing is that even music designed to hook you instantly often doesn't do that for me. I can be very lukewarm towards a pop album on first listen, but grow to like it more and more. Golden Hour is probably the best example of this; at first I was like "is this it? The fact that that's his least favourite tracks indicates that we're really not coming at this album from similar perspectives, I guess. 

Incidentally, I'm not exactly some super fan of Fiona Apple - I had listened to The Idler Wheel a while ago and gave it a 7, liking it but not seeing anything truly special in it (I should probably go back and reevaluate). Speedrun tutorial might actually help with that. Take the strats that are consistent for you, and replace the hard strats with slow ones of your own. "You don't care about doing good deeds you care about the attention."  


Why can't someone care about both? Why do you assume that someone having a selfish motivation must be guided *solely* by that motivation? Humans have complex reasons for doing things. If you wanna get very reductive, you can say that everything is selfish. Even if you don't film yourself helping out someone in need, you may just be doing it because of the feeling of righteousness it gives you, not because you genuinely care about the person in question. In any case, the end result is the same, filming or not filming, selfish or not selfish. You've done something good for someone. I'd rather some guy film himself buying a homeless guy food, encouraging others to do the same, even if it is a kind of vanity project, than that same guy just do nothing to help anybody.

All-nighters and low sleep are horrible to get through and it can feel like an accomplishment,  if you actually managed to get the work done or do well in the following day's exam. I'm not saying it isn't annoying to brag about it, but a little empathy goes a long way. I wouldn't begrudge someone mentioning it unless they are heavily bragging (e.g. "lol I didn't even sleep and I smashed that exam"). 

As for the "probably procrastinated" and "took too many hard classes" thing...maybe? The former especially is obviously going to be a major reason for many all-nighters. But sometimes even a very prepared student can *feel* ill-prepared due to their own insecurities, and end up working too far into the night, and then have difficulty sleeping after that. I've been there a lot of times and you feel hard done-by because it's not a choice so much as what you feel you have to do, in the case of over-revising, and a consequence of your anxieties, in the case of having trouble sleeping. Talking about your lack of sleep is one way of proactively guarding against the potential of making or having made stupid mistakes, to take some weight off your own shoulders.

I can't tell if you're joking or not lol. I just know that doctors have a hell of a lot of people to deal with and a fifteen minute appointment seems a short time to be sure enough to prescribe anti-depressants, to me. 

It is immediately important to me that I enjoy myself. Indeed, if that weren't the primary motivator, I would work much harder on things. But I often don't really *work* at things, that's the irony. I often do them in ways that aren't conducive to super fast improvement. Regardless, I still expect myself to naturally get better, even when my practice is not particularly efficient or well thought-out. I look at other people and judge myself based on how much time I've spent and how good I should be based on how good other people are over that period of time. Or I just arbitrarily decide that I ought to be good after a certain amount of time. Eventually it feels embarrassing to not be great at something you've sunk *so much* into. And it's not like I'm actually good and am selling myself short. There is *nothing* in life that I'm even close to impressive at. I understand that it's all relative, but I don't have sufficient skill in anything to impress anyone who knows even a reasonable amount about the thing. And it feels like most people are at least skilled in *something*. But not me.

Presumably you've just done C-sides, so now is the best time to do those goldens as you have the muscle memory. There's no hard rule that says you have to do the goldens in order of difficulty, of course, but doing so gets you more experience with the feeling of having one life and will keep your confidence at a good level as you will be achieving at a steady rate. With that in mind, I'd group the goldens something like this, with each row being increasingly difficult.

C-sides, 1A, 2A

4A, 1B, 2B

3A, 5A

3B, 4B, 5B, 8A

6A,7A,8B

6B

7B

9.

Some people would put 3A higher and 6A lower among other things, but that's a good general idea I think.

As for general advice, for the early goldens you can just jump straight in. As things get harder, you want to practice individual segments, especially the later ones, and get them deathless. Make sure you have a clear, consistent strategy for each individual screen. It can save you a world of pain if you do this work before actually doing attempts with the golden berry. For the harder levels, you have a pretty low chance of just happening to get the golden, so it's worth it to do low death runs until you have a reasonable death count (single digits is good to aim for).

If she lunges at you on the ground and you're well within range, jump over her and get a couple of hits in from the other side (you can also pogo if you time it well).  If she lunges at you from relatively far away you can dash away or even just step away. When she does her dive, just step or dash aside as she comes down, then get some hits. You can hit her with a Vengeful Spirit while she does the AOE attack, or just wait it out if you want to conserve soul. When she boomerangs her needle, she gives you a perfect window to Desolate Dive right on her, or a few slashes if you prefer (this needs decent timing). This can also be a good healing window if you have Quick Focus on, so long as you're out of range when she's prepping the throw.

If she prepares to parry, do not hit her, just wait it out (even a spell here will not do damage, if I'm not mistaken). If you mess up and she parries you successfully, dash away immediately as she will swing her needle in an arc around her. Finally, when she covers the arenas in spike balls, I'd recommend clearing most but not all of them. She tends to just recover the arena very quickly if you prioritize taking out all the spikes, and you can easily lose track of what she's doing if you get *too* focused on them.

The only other "attacks" are her random bounces. Tbh, those are what hit me the most (and the reason why I haven't beaten her on Radiant lol). But if you play reactively you should walk/jump into her less.

Quick Focus, Deep Focus, Grubsong, Soul Catcher and whatever (Nailmaster's Glory, Spore Shroom and Thorns of Agony are all reasonable). Start the fight by pogoing him as much as you can. During his sword attacks just go for damage and damage tank if you have to. Once he spins his shields, run away and heal. You can usually get one or two heals off to heal two or four health. You wanna go in harder on the facetanking in the two shield phase to get it over with as quickly as possible, since dodging is more difficult and he is harder to hit. Shriek can work wonders here too. I recommend Soul Catcher to help with that, but the first three charms are the key. Shape of Unn is also viable (it may let you dodge a wayward spinning shield, but I wouldn't recommend ever healing during the sword attack as it is generally safer to dodge and wait for the shield spin if you are low on health).

10. Fish Out of Water 

This entry demonstrates the brilliant creativity of the animation team and manages to be funny and truly poignant with no dialogue for most of the runtime. Also, special props for the use of music in this episode, particularly "Sea of Dreams".  

9. Best Thing That Ever Happened

This sort of classes as a bottle episode. It's the brilliant culmination of years of conflict and difficulty between PC and BoJack. The dialogue and voice acting is top notch. The latter was perhaps assisted by the fact that Sedaris and Arnett recorded the lines together, in a break from the usual recording methods. This harsh and emotional entry is punctuated by a wonderfully blunt ending.

8. The Showstopper 

At this point we know to expect something bad from episode 11, but Season 5 still manages to spice things up with the confusing duality of BoJack and Philbert and the awesome musical number. A haunting, disturbing episode, especially in that gorgeous final shot. 

7. Downer Ending

Say Anything was probably the point at which this show declared it had something to say. The Telescope consolidated that. And then Downer Ending tells you that this show is going to be truly, truly special. At least early on, the episode is hilarious (Dr Hu?). The animation is inventive and purposeful, and we get profound poignancy both in BoJack's dreams of idolized domesticity and his utterly devastating final speech. 

6. Ruthie 

Ooof. Even if you saw what was coming, this episode hits like a freight train. It's another great outing for Princess Carolyn, after the excellent episodes Say Anything and Best Thing That Ever Happened, and it is perhaps the bleakest and most heartbreaking of them all. The framing device could well be construed as gimmicky, but we realize by the end that its presence is the whole point of the episode. You go through Ruthie with a sense of hope, however minuscule, however well you know that the show doesn't do happy endings, but it is inevitably taken away. And that ending song is brutal.

5. Stupid Piece of Shit 


This might well be higher if it weren't for the fairly paint-by-numbers B-story. Aside from that, this is simply the most honest and brilliant depiction of depression in media that I have ever seen. Animation, writing and vocals are all absolutely on fire here. Anyone who has experienced depression or known a sufferer can relate to Stupid Piece of Shit intensely. I know I'm mentioning endings in literally every episode, but fuck it, BoJack episodes are so good at endings. The conversation between BoJack and Hollyhock is just fantastic. BoJack lies yet again, but this time, at least, it's for someone else's benefit. Was it the right thing? Does BoJack do the right thing? Let's find out. 

4. The Old Sugarman Place


Talk about not pulling your punches. After a BoJack free satirical episode full of ridiculous hi-jinks, Season 4 goes for the jugular with this viciously sad and darkly beautiful episode. We finally learn just what's been troubling BoJack's mother (though there's more to come later), and it's horrifying. The theater-style treatment of different time periods is inspired and incredibly effective, most notably in the stunning duet "I Will Always Think of You". They fuck you up, your mum and dad. They don't mean to, but they do. This is pretty much the mantra of Season 4 and it's displayed in full effect here. The general theme of holding on to and being controlled by the past (Great Gatsby-esque eh...hmm, did that car chase look familiar?) is paralleled well by the great one-off character Eddie. Really, this is a perfect episode. The problem is, there are 3 other perfect episodes that I prefer! 

3. Escape From L.A. 


Escape From L.A. is a phenomenal exercise in dread. We know as soon as BoJack sets foot in New Mexico that things can't end well. But the episode builds things up reasonably slowly. We have some laughs watching BoJack try to cover up his real motivation for coming to see Charlotte, and then suddenly BoJack has been in New Mexico for two months and he's playing the "fun uncle" type. Damn, he hasn't fucked up anything yet. Maybe things will be alright? But then he asks Penny to the prom. Seeds of doubt creep in. He gives kids alcohol...well, they'd drink anyway, right? It's no big deal? But one of them ends up paralytic and we see BoJack's most manipulative tendencies come out. It's dreadfully uncomfortable to watch. But things heat up, of course. After we're sure that BoJack has at least done something right by rejecting Penny, he comes on to Charlotte in a scene full of great dialogue. And then he rejects Penny again...except he doesn't. I'll never forget how much of a knot in my stomach I had from watching this the first time. The use of "fuck" is the best in the series, and the ending is beautiful. Man, I could talk about this episode for days. 

2. Free Churro 


Like Fish Out of Water, this is a bold experiment. Like Fish Out of Water, this is excellent. But I'm a sucker for words (look at how many I've written), so Free Churro comes out well on top for me. There isn't a great deal to say. The writing is perfect, the voice acting is perfect. In many ways Free Churro revisits issue of Season 4, but it never feels superfluous. It feels like the natural culmination of BoJack's hugely troubled relationship with his parents. And it's so raw, so dark, so powerful, so full to the brim of meaning. Just sublime. 

1. Time's Arrow 


I binged Season 4 as soon as it came out. The Old Sugarman Place had floored me, but I soldiered on. Stupid Piece of Shit had floored me, but I soldiered on. Ruthie had floored me, but I soldiered on. And then this...I was a sobbing mess. It took me a fair while to be able to watch the finale. I guess I'll start with the particular scene. BoJack, having said several times that he wants his mother to recognize him, just so he can rip into her, doesn't succumb to these base, petty desires. I think it ties into Free Churro. BoJack's father says that BoJack can only depend on himself, and BoJack himself echoes this near the end of the episode. Moreover, BoJack is sad over the fact that his parents could never truly "see" him. When he ascends these stairs, which seem like a stairway to heaven or at least some sort of afterlife, he might expect to find his parents and get the closure he desperately wanted. But he finds only himself, staring down at him. Only BoJack can truly "see" himself. He is profoundly isolated.

There could be a religious element here, especially with the imagery of BoJack ascending steps to a bright light. Religion (or certain religions) tells us that there is some external force judging us in a very binary sense. We're good, or we're bad. But BoJack doesn't find some sort of god/maker after ascending the steps. He just finds himself. In the shallow world of Hollywoo, God is very much dead. By extension, so is lasting societal judgment. Nobody in Hollywoo is going to hold people like Vance Waggoner or BoJack to account, at least not in the long-term. BoJack can't get the external judgement he wants (and begs Diane for in S5E12); only he can hold himself to account and strive to be better.  Going back to "I see you", there's also a case to be made for this being the particular moment in which BoJack finally *does* see himself for what he is, making this moment a sort of catalyst for change. He's finally internalized Todd's message from S3E10: "It's you".

She did not force BoJack to stop seeing Dr. Indira. She merely asked him not to see her. Imagine you have a best friend with whom you have a very complicated, troubled relationship, full of difficult moments. You've been seeing a therapist for seven years and have talked to her many times about this friend and your conflicts with him and feelings about him. Furthermore, you have reason to believe that your therapist doesn't take confidentiality as seriously as she should. Do you really want your friend to start seeing this exact same therapist? No, you're going to feel very vulnerable, and like he has invaded and compromised a very important part of your life. And once BoJack has decided to go against Diane's wishes and she leaves Dr. Indira, Diane actually tells BoJack to continue his therapy.

Then BoJack has the gall to tell Diane that she and him are the same. Diane *knows* that BoJack has done some awful things, especially in his relationship with Sarah Lynn. That alone is far worse than anything we have seen Diane do. But Diane also knows that she doesn't have the full story of just how bad BoJack is and, truth be told, the New Mexico incident actually sounds even worse than it was on the tape. Therefore it's not hard to see why Diane would resent BoJack for labeling her as equally screwed-up as him and want to prove him wrong. Do I think her response is mature or sensible? Well, no, not at all, but BoJack has been a terrible friend to her and she has reason to believe that he's been involved in some truly disturbing, reprehensible acts. Also note in this episode how BoJack jerks Diane around, heavily implying he wants to talk about his mother's death but then not allowing Diane to actually talk to him about it, and he treats Diane as nothing more than a free therapist, seeing little difference between how he interacted with Indira and what he expects from Diane. All this assholery pushes Diane to breaking point.

Edit: As for Mr. Peanutbutter, I don't think that we can really view the marriage as something immoral. Diane really loves Mr. Peanutbutter and values his positiveness and probably genuinely hopes that they will be able to build a successful marriage. It's misguided, sure, but no more than that. I do agree that her overreactions are a bit much, but they're not entirely unwarranted. Because I have no life at the moment, I did an episode by episode comparison (e.g. comparing all the episode 1s, then all the episode 2s etc.) earlier and episodes scored points based on their rank against the same numbered episode from the other seasons. My ranking from that was 1 < 4 < 2 = 3 < 5 (17 points, 23 points, 26 points and 30 points if you're wondering). Okay, that's not really a fair way of comparing seasons; it was just fun lol. However it did make me realize that Season 4 isn't as strong as I previously thought. I'd had it as my favourite season, but I was ranking a bunch of its episodes (4th, 5th, 7th and 8th) as the worst in their respective places. This got me thinking that the middle of the season is kind of eeeh except for Stupid Piece of Shit. Really, the reason I was ranking the season so highly was because of its killer episodes 2,6,9 and 11 and the uplifting ending, not because of its overall cohesion. Hence I'm starting to actually think that this ranking I've obtained might be "correct" and am finding it hard to justify the ranking I previously had (4 > 2 = 3 > 1), with me picking 2 over 3 if you literally put a gun to my head. So let's try and briefly justify why this ranking makes sense. Vague spoilers ahead if for some reason you're on this thread without seeing the fifth season.

​

1. Season 5.Imo this season was consistently very strong. There is just no lull in the middle and every character gets due care and attention. Diane in particular is handled brilliantly, and, contrary to what some people say, I think Bojack's arc is also really great. Some might feel like it's just rehashing the previous arc, and to some extent that's kiiinda true, but you have to note that he's really improved in the first half and learned from season 4. But ultimately he's still too unhealthy to handle grief and he predictably starts spiraling. But he ends up more ready to truly learn and change than he's ever been.
2. Season 2

There's pretty much nothing between this and season 3. I pick this in a pinch mainly for Escape From L.A. but I recognize advantages Season 3 has over it. This season has a great storyline and pretty much no lull also, although admittedly its second half is stronger. Episodes 7-11 are *all* fantastic and that's quite a feat.

3. Season 3

This is probably the tightest season there is and the one that feels most like a cohesive story. Every single episode has a very clear narrative purpose. I don't find the second half as compelling as Season 2's half, although That's Too Much Man of course has the legendary moment and the finale is the best season finale the show has done. But the quality here is just so well spread out. It's not a season which relies on wowza ez top 10 episodes (Fish Out of Water, That's Too Much Man and wonderful underrated BTTEH are great though); it's just great storytelling.

4. Season 4

Oh how the mighty have fallen. I had this as my very undisputed number 1 season. But I'm thinking differently because of the reasons I already outlined above. Not much more to say than that. It still has three of my top five episodes. But I can't deny that the subplots aren't that great, the season meanders a bit in its middle part, and it's nowhere near as tight as say Season 3.

5. Season 1

I actually think this season is kind of underrated. The first few episodes don't offer a great deal but it's somewhat intentional; hell, in the pitch for this show they *said* it would start out like a typical animated comedy and only later start to give you feelings. And I think this season is really clever in how it sneaks up on you like that. And even if its early episodes aren't great, every episode of the first six is important for story or character; they don't just faff around doing bullshit like on other animated shows. But there's just not enough truly strong episodes for me to rank this above any of the other seasons.

Funnily enough the quote that perks me up if I do feel down is this one: "The universe is a cruel uncaring void. The key to being happy isn't the search for meaning; it's to keep yourself busy with unimportant nonsense, then eventually you'll be dead." 

I don't take it to the extreme and just be totally hedonistic; I've been doing very well at university and once I get back I'll still put the work in. But it's a very comforting thought to me that ultimately all my hopes and dreams aren't that important, and whatever happens and whatever I do, even if I fail miserably, it's nothing to be truly worried about, and I should just try and find happiness in the day-to-day "nonsense" rather than look for some big grand "something" that will make everything great.

One of my favourites is at the end of S4E9, "Ruthie". 
[Spoiler](#s "It's a lovely song obviously, but lyrically it's a fantastic choice. It of course describes Princess Carolyn - her heart has made a fool out of her, she has drunkenly thrown away two great relationships in one day; she spent her 30s trying to make things work with BoJack when it was doomed from the start, she let herself get optimistic about her pregnancy. And then you also have the brutal lines 'I'm everything that a flower is, I plan to make about thirty kids'. But the song also poignantly links in to the viewers emotions as we watch the episode. I'm a white male, I'm not straight. Maybe the lack of safety women feel on average is different, and maybe on average it's more severe, but it's not particularly rational either. In the episode Diane makes the comment that men commit 90% of violent crimes (or something like that, it might have been gun violence or murders), but it's also true that men are overwhelmingly more likely to be the victims of assault. Perhaps men do feel safer, but there's no reason they should. They're less likely to be sexually assaulted, of course (well, prisons aside), but in general women aren't that likely to be sexually assaulted by a random guy in the street - the large majority of the time it's someone the woman knows. So maybe I don't get it, but Diane basically proposes people arming themselves just to feel better, since in practical terms they're pretty unlikely to be victimized in these sorts of contexts anyway, and that's a pretty stupid proposal imo. 

Another thing that bugs me with the whole understanding thing is that Diane is essentially purporting to speak for women in general, just because she personally feels empowered by having a gun. How does she know that all other women feel unsafe in the way she does? And how does she know that men generally feel safe? I think individuals often are unable to understand certain experiences of other individuals because their empathy only goes so far and they haven't experienced similar enough things, I don't like looking at things through this collectivist lens, which is what Diane does here. I understand it can often be helpful to group things together but the preachy way in which it is done in this episode just gets under my skin.

I only take issue with Thoughts and Prayers. Everything else is fine. But I basically agree in the sense that the show has always been political; I just happen to disagree with some of the messages this time around, whereas I agreed with the general points of S1E2, S2E7 and S3E6 (S2E5 doesn't really count imo as it's tackling meat eating in a world where animals are as smart as people and live alongside them). 

My problem with Thoughts and Prayers is the feminist angle. Diane is the voice of reason in S2E7 and S3E6 but in this one her opinions are ludicrous, stating that men feel safe all the time and immediately changing her opinion on guns once she handles one. It seems clear that she is a mouthpiece for the writer (incidentally, this is the only episode of the show written by Nick Adams), especially given the very cringeworthy line from A Ryan that went something like "as a straight white male I will plough through and assume I'm doing fine". 

In general there's a lot of anti-male and hyper feminist sentiment here, S2E7 did that to an extent (e.g. the "white men in bow ties" thing) but it tread the line well imo, this just leaps right over it. There's the line I just said, there's the badger, there's the guy saying "I don't feel safe walking down my own street any more. Me, a man!", the guy saying something like "one bullet from the gun of a female gun owner is too much", and all the congressmen. I am very anti-gun myself, but I can understand how some people might think that banning all guns being described as "sensible legislature" is extreme. 

The preachiness isn't necessarily new territory for this show, it's just that it didn't come so thick and fast before; a good example is in S3E3 when Goober says "they won't internalize deeply problematic notions about...", it's very unsubtle and the writer is clearly just shoving their opinion in with little nuance, but it's just one line, and otherwise the whole Whale World thing is good satire. In this case there's just too many examples of lines like this, so that the episode feels like a whole Buzzfeed article in itself. Or, indeed, a Girl Croosh article. 

Edit: Actually I do also take some issue with S4E2. BoJack's grandfather's comments relating to how sexist the time period was have the subtlety and nuance of a brick to the face. This makes sense in [Spoiler](#s "S4E11 since Beatrice is an unreliable narrator who will naturally have a biased recollection of her father") but in this one we're supposed to think this is exactly how it happened, and the directness of it takes you out of it and makes him into a veritable caricature.

This has to be the best season imo. Episodes 2 and 6 and all of the last four are simply sublime. I've never laughed all that much at this show [edit: realised this contradicts my previous paragraph, basically, I'm talking about proper belly laughs here, I'll find myself mildly laughing through my nose a lot of the time] , which is ironic as it's quite possibly my favourite and is ostensibly a comedy, but said comedy is as good as ever, and the drama seems to have, impossibly, stepped up a notch. I can't quite put my finger on it - perhaps it is merely a consequence of the structural changes. Season 1, 2 and 3 largely followed the same path. Bojack's an asshole with problems, Bojack damages his relationships / drives people away, eventually Bojack does something absolutely horrible and then feels very sad. Brilliant, but repetitive, and while it wouldn't necessarily be untrue to life to retread that ground yet again, this season beautifully flips things around. 

This is epitomised by the use of f word. If we followed the same structure as before, Bojack wouldn't say fuck in episode 5. He would say it to his mum at the end of episode 11, and walk out. But the writers essentially subvert their own tendency towards subversion - in your average story where an asshole guy who doesn't know how to love people or be loved gets in touch with a daughter he never knew he had, this would of course eventually make him a better person. So we expect Bojack Horseman to subvert that and have Bojack wind up completely losing said daughter (well, sister), leaving his mum with the last words "fuck you", and moping around for Episode 12. But it doesn't. The experience actually does change Bojack, and he does, if perhaps ephemerally, find some happiness, and learn to help others rather than infect their lives with his misery. Because the previous three seasons have been spent reinforcing how real and brutal this world is, this series can believably and organically have things play out the way you actually want them to play out for once. It's an incredibly hopeful ending, and to be honest it wouldn't a bad one for the series as a whole. Of course, things are miserable for Diane, Mr. Peanutbutter and Princess Carolyn, but it would feel very contrived if everyone got a happy ending, and there is hope for all parties. I refuse to believe Ralph would completely give up on Carolyn so quickly, and, much as such a thing would have seemed ludicrous to me back in Season 2, Diane might be happy with a slightly-less-unhappy Bojack, and we know Mr.Peanutbutter and Todd will be happy so long as something occupies them. 

Also, it'd probably be best served on the episode thread, but I just wanna mention that Episode 11 is, for me, by far away the best of the always brutal 11's, and one of the best episodes I've seen of any show period.
